newsitem.title: FRANCE: AGF not ruled out as bid target-analysts.
newsitem.headline: AGF not ruled out as bid target-analysts.

text.p: Germany's Deutsche Bank may have dismissed on Wednesday a report that it plans to buy French insurer AGF but financial analysts do not rule out the idea it could be a bid target.
Fuelling the speculation has been the consolidation under way in Europe's financial sector, highlighted by the merger this week of Swiss bank Credit Suisse and Swiss insurer Winterhur.
"AGF has been doing a great job at getting its property problems sorted out and getting its earnings back on track for recovery," said one London-based analyst.
"Its shares are not very expensive and so if the market does not acknowledge its progress, perhaps a predator might," he said.

AGF shares opened up 2.08 percent after the German daily Die Welt said that Deutche Bank wanted to take over the insurer. The report had followed a statement by Deutsche Bank chief executive Rolf Breuer last month that his bank was considering making an acquisition in France.

The shares retraced after Deutsche Bank called the report "pure speculation" but then recovered to trade up 0.88 percent at 218.40 francs by late afternoon in the face of an overall market down more than two percent.
The gain in heavy volume of more than one million shares traded followed a 2.1 percent rise on Tuesday. One brokerage house calculated this week AGF shares had a "theoretical" value of 260 francs.
Some analysts said Wednesday's rise was due partly to first half figures released after the market closed on Tuesday showing AGF's premium income rose 5.9 percent to 35.74 billion francs.

"The figures show they are holding up well in the overall climate but there is no doubt there are people out there taking speculative positions on the possibility a bid may come along," said a Paris analyst.
Last year's takeover by French insurer Axa of rival UAP, creating the world's second largest insurer, was seen as a sign of more consolidation to come as insurers chase critical mass to cut costs.
Looming European monetary union, due to go into effect in 1999, is also expected to make a strong presence in several European markets desirable to some insurers.
And the Credit Suisse-Winterhur merger has given a boost to the concept of bancassurance -- sale of insurance products through banks.
AGF has most frequently been mentioned as a predator -- it has said it is interested in acquiring state-controlled insurer GAN when it is privatised.

The European Commission, which has stipulated GAN must be sold in exchange for clearing 20 billion francs ($3.2 billion) in state aid to the insurer, battling to recover from property woes, has said the sale must take place by June 30 next year.

Some analysts say a failure by AGF to win GAN, could make it especially vulnerable to a bid. Several firms, including German insurer Allianz and insurance group Eureko, have also expressed interest in GAN.

AGF chairman Antoine Jeancourt-Galignani told a Senate hearing in May that he "would not give much for AGF's independence within two or three years" without GAN, according to an official account of his appearance.
Jeancourt-Galignani warned, however, that any bid for AGF would be "necessarily hostile" which he said was traditionally tough to pull off in the insurance business.
AGF believes it has the jump over its rivals for GAN because it is a French insurer, enjoys strong synergies and a common corporate culture with GAN.
If AGF fails in its quest for GAN, overshadowed at home by the AXA-UAP mega-merger, it "must conclude an alliance," said one Paris analyst.
-- Paris Newsroom +33 1 4221 5452 ($ = 6.280 French Francs)
